extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent drafters, patent agents, patent attorneys, and technical professionals preparing patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing, drafting, filing and prosecuting patent applications, with detailed criteria for claim drafting, preparing descriptions/drawings/abstracts, prosecution strategies, and organizational procedures. Emphasizes both theory and practical drafting skills across many technologies and jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a patent, claims must typically be for an invention that is new (novel), involves inventive step/nonobviousness, and is industrially applicable (useful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art encompasses all knowledge available to the public at the filing date. Different jurisdictions may use synonymous but not identical terms (e.g., 'nonobvious' for inventive step). Also consider patentable subject matter exclusions and local definitions of 'technical'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirement (sufficiency of disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent application must disclose the invention sufficiently clearly and completely that a person skilled in the art can carry out the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the description supports the full scope of the claims; avoid leaving claims that cannot be practiced. Disclosure must enable reduction to practice where required by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the subject matter is eligible for patent protection (products, processes, chemical compositions, biotechnology, computer-implemented inventions, etc.) under the applicable law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of jurisdictional exclusions (e.g., pure mathematical algorithms, mere nucleic acid sequences without function, certain methods of treatment). Draft claims to emphasize technical/functional aspects where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: File before public disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application must be filed before publicly disclosing any important research results that may destroy novelty in countries where protection is sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should set up internal publication clearance procedures to review journal and conference submissions. Preserve priority/filing dates accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing invention disclosures and identifying patentable inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain complete invention disclosures from inventors that identify the field, technical problem, closest related art, advantages, drawings and written description, inventors and dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an invention disclosure form (Annex B) capturing background, related art, public disclosures, testing dates, contributors, and document attachments to determine patentability and inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical parts of a patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application typically includes a request, description, claims, drawings, abstract and must follow the applicable application format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow required formalities for each jurisdiction. Order of drafting may vary but consider drafting claims early to focus the description and embodiments around the claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare the claims first
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing an application, draft the claims first to identify the core inventive concept and guide the drafting of the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting claims early helps frame the invention, avoid omissions and ensures the description supports all claimed subject matter. Use claim language to capture different protection layers (broad/narrow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of the patent claim (role and structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are sets of sentences that define the invention being protected; they determine the scope of exclusive rights conferred by a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand parts of a claim (preamble, body, characterizing portion), grammar and conventions (two-part form, transitional phrases), and how claim language maps to potential infringing acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad and narrow claims (claim scope layering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a combination of broad claims to maximize coverage and narrow claims to increase allowance prospects and fallback positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance breadth with patentability. Broad claims must still be supported by disclosure and withstand prior art; include dependent and fallback claims to preserve value during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim grammar and word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clear, consistent, and jurisdiction-appropriate claim wording, paying attention to transitional phrases like 'comprising' and their intended effect (open/closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include description language to clarify whether terms like 'comprise' are intended to be inclusive. Avoid ambiguous or inconsistent terminology between claims and description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part (improvement) claims and claim formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-part claims (e.g., Jepson-style) separate known features from the distinguishing features; various claim formats (product, method, use) should be used where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two-part form in jurisdictions that recognize it; select claim types (product, process, parameter, product-by-process, medical indication, composition, biotechnology, computer-implemented) suited to the invention and strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative elements, Markush and functional claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft claims that allow alternative elements (Markush groups) and functional language where appropriate, while complying with jurisdictional rules on clarity and support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Markush claims for chemical/compound alternatives; be cautious with functional/means-plus-function language because many jurisdictions construe such claims narrowly and require corresponding disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and dependent claims; claim sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize claim sets with independent claims defining principal scopes and dependent claims adding further limitations as fallbacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the number and structure of independent claims permitted by the jurisdiction, use dependent claims to preserve fallback positions, and avoid unnecessary duplication. Multiple dependent claims have special rules/costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple dependent claims refer to more than one previous claim and are governed by specific formal and fee rules in many jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple dependent claims sparingly and in compliance with local rules (fees, format). Consider drafting alternatives if jurisdiction disallows or penalizes multiple dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce limitations into claims that are not essential to distinguish over the prior art or to practice the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unnecessary limitations narrow protection and provide easy workarounds for competitors; use careful drafting to capture the inventive concept broadly while retaining support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative limitations and disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative limitations (claiming what the invention is not) and disclaimers may be used but have special support/allowability considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use disclaimers only when supported or permitted (e.g., to avoid prior art) and be mindful of jurisdictional rules on added matter and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must overcome prior art (anticipation and obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be drafted to distinguish over known prior art so that they are novel and involve an inventive step/nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct thorough prior-art searches (patent and scientific databases) and draft claims and description to emphasize distinguishing technical features and advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensuring the description supports the claims (original disclosure/new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must provide support for the claimed subject matter; amendments adding new matter not originally disclosed are not allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting and amending, ensure the claimed scope has basis in the original disclosure; carefully document embodiments and alternatives to preserve amendment latitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in an application should comply with unity requirements—claims should relate to a single inventive concept or be linked by a common inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider unity when choosing claim scope or filing divisional applications where multiple inventions are present; follow PCT and national rules on unity to avoid objections or additional fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim point of view (claim drafting perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft claims from the point of view of what needs to be protected and what competitors might do; consider infringement scenarios when choosing claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate how courts and patent offices will construe claim language; draft to capture likely implementation variants and to reduce ambiguity at enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing a patent claim during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend claims during prosecution to overcome objections or prior art, but be mindful of limits on adding new matter and on broadening amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dependent claims as fallbacks; understand jurisdictional rules on broadening vs narrowing, and maintain support in the original disclosure for any amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction in the courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims will be interpreted by courts to determine infringement and validity, so drafting must anticipate likely constructions and how claim language maps to embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear definitions in the description, avoid inconsistent usage, and consider including exemplary embodiments that illustrate claimed features to guide claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting a description: title, technical field, background and summary
rubrics_metrics.description: The description should include a clear title, technical field, background art describing prior problems, and a summary of the invention highlighting advantages and core inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The background should disclose closest prior art and problems solved; the summary should make the inventive contribution clear and align with claim language so description supports claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting embodiments and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide detailed embodiments and examples that illustrate how to practice the invention and variants that fall within the claimed scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sufficient detail (materials, parameters, methods) for enablement and consider covering alternatives and fallback variants to preserve claim breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare drawings of appropriate types with reference indicators and a suitable level of detail to illustrate embodiments and aid claim interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate reference numerals between drawings and description; decide whether inventor-provided drawings are sufficient and supplement where necessary to show inventive features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting an abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a concise abstract summarizing the invention for publication purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract should be brief and informative but not used to limit claim scope; follow jurisdictional length and content rules for abstracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from patentability and industrial applicability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify statutory exclusions and ensure the invention meets the requirement of industrial applicability (utility) where required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to excluded subject matter in particular jurisdictions (e.g., some countries exclude methods of treatment, discoveries, mathematical methods) and draft claims to emphasize technical application and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple claim types for the same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Include different claim types (product, process/method, use, apparatus) for the same inventive concept to maximize protection and enforcement options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft parallel claim sets (device+method) when appropriate, and ensure the description supports each claim type with enabling disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments and prosecution practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond to office actions, draft responses, perform interviews, and manage amendments, paying attention to deadlines, appeals, divisional/continuation/CIP filings and opposition proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare principled amendment strategies that preserve value, justify claim changes with support in the original disclosure, and use interviews to resolve examiner objections when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining original disclosure and new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: When amending, determine whether added or amended content is supported by the original filing to avoid introducing new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear records of original descriptions and embodiments; when in doubt, prefer narrowing amendments that are clearly supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent office procedures, filing routes and fees (domestic, priority, PCT, EPO, USPTO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the appropriate filing procedures for domestic, priority, foreign, and international (PCT) filings, and be mindful of patent office procedures and fee structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PCT for international priority; consult Module VIII for jurisdiction-specific filing requirements (USPTO, EPO) and consider cost implications for prosecution in multiple countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search and prior-art resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct prior-art searches using patent databases, national/regional office databases and scientific/technical databases to identify relevant prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarize with PATENTSCOPE, national databases, and field-specific scientific databases; search broadly because prior art includes non-patent literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent strategy: offensive and defensive patenting; design-around
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt patenting strategies such as offensive blocking patents, defensive patenting, and design-around techniques to serve business goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on strategy based on commercial objectives, competitive landscape and enforcement capacity; consider portfolio-building, cross-licensing and standards-essential patent implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing, educating and motivating the technical team
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement training for management, marketing and technical staff on patent significance; set up invention disclosure and review committees and inventor incentive programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide patent-drafting and disclosure training, establish periodic patent review committees to evaluate disclosures, and design incentives to encourage reporting and accurate inventor identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional ethics and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe professional ethics in patent drafting and filings; understand representation rules in jurisdictions for who may represent applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that some jurisdictions restrict representation to registered patent agents/attorneys; maintain confidentiality, correct inventorship, and avoid conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention disclosure form completeness (procedural checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention disclosure forms should capture title, field, background, closest related art, advantages, drawings availability, written description, inventor details, testing dates, publications, disclosures, trade shows and comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect attachments (published articles, NDAs, drawings), document internal and external disclosures, and sign/witness the form to preserve priority and enable drafting decisions.
